big_idea: Two small groups can compose into one bigger, or decompose. We compare with MORE, LESS, or EQUAL.
learning_intention: We are learning to build a target number lots of different ways using cubes, then to compare two groups and decide whether the first has MORE than, LESS than, or is EQUAL to the second.
student_learning_goal: I can build a number lots of different ways and compare two groups using more, less, or equal.
success_criteria: I can build the number 7 using two different combinations of cubes (for example 4 and 3, or 5 and 2).
I can decompose a group of 7 cubes into two smaller groups in two different ways.
I can compare two plates of objects and circle MORE / LESS / EQUAL with a reason ('this plate has 6, this plate has 4 — 6 is more than 4').
I can use the words MORE, LESS, and EQUAL correctly when I talk about my partner's plate.
lesson_specific_materials: Two-colour linking cubes (red and yellow), at least 10 of each colour per child
Comparison strip (M6) — two parallel sentence-strip rows for visual side-by-side comparing — one per partner pair
A small basket per pair with two paper plates labelled PLATE A and PLATE B
Tim Hortons-style timbit counters or paper-circle 'cookies' (~30 per pair) for the cookie-plate comparison
Number cards 0-10 (M4), one set per pair, used to randomly draw target compose numbers
Three big circle cards labelled MORE, LESS, EQUAL, for the whole-class anchor
Anchor chart paper labelled 'Building 7' on the left and 'Comparing Plates' on the right with MORE / LESS / EQUAL columns

minds_on.hook: Buddy has TWO plates of bones — he wants the plate with MORE. Which one is it?
minds_on.teacher_script: Bring children to the carpet. Hold up Buddy and two plates: 'Plate A has 6 bones. Plate B has 4 bones. Buddy wants MORE — which plate?' Affirm: 'Six is MORE than four. Four is LESS than six.' Lay out MORE / LESS / EQUAL cards.
student_actions: Sit in a half-circle facing the two paper plates.
Help compare 6 vs. 4 bones using the words MORE and LESS.
Help compare 3 vs. 3 bones and discover the new word EQUAL.
Watch the teacher build 7 two different ways with red and yellow cubes.
Notice that the same number can be built more than one way.

action.activity_name: Building 7 Lots of Ways, Then Comparing Plates

steps.instruction: Whole-group compose demo with target number 7. The class chants 'we are building seven, in lots of ways'. The teacher invites four children up one at a time. Each child uses red and yellow cubes to build 7 a different way and snaps the tower onto a long horizontal track on the easel. Likely contributions: 0+7, 1+6, 2+5, 3+4. Class chants the matching addition fact each time ('zero and seven is seven'). Teacher records each composition on the 'Building 7' anchor column with a coloured icon: red square + yellow square + total.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say: 'Friends, our target is SEVEN. Build it any way you like with red and yellow cubes. Take any number of red — even zero — and add yellows until you have seven.' Watch for the child who builds 7+0 and lift it up: 'Look — Carla used zero red and seven yellow. That STILL makes seven. Zero is a real number too.'

steps.instruction: Partner compose station. Each pair has a number card deck (0-10), two-colour cubes, and a ten-frame each. Partner A draws a card (e.g., 8). Both partners build that number two different ways on their own ten-frames. Then they swap towers and check each other's count. Repeat with three or four target numbers. The teacher walks the room with the formative checklist; children who build TWO valid combinations for each number are securely composing on A6.5.
steps.teacher_prompt: At the pair: 'Show me your ten-frame. You drew 8. Build it one way — got it? Now build it a DIFFERENT way. The total is still 8 but the colours are different.' For struggling children: 'Take 8 cubes total. Pull off 2 cubes — how many are left? 6. So 2 and 6 makes 8. Try another split.'

steps.instruction: Switch to compare station with cookie plates and the comparison strip. Each pair gets two paper plates and ~30 paper cookies. Partner A makes a plate (any number 1-10). Partner B makes a different plate. They line the cookies up on the comparison strip — Plate A's row above, Plate B's row below — so the visual side-by-side is unmistakable. Then they pick the right circle card: MORE / LESS / EQUAL. Each pair completes at least four rounds, switching who makes which plate.
steps.teacher_prompt: At the pair: 'Line them up so each cookie on top has a buddy below — what's left over tells you the answer. If the top row has extras, top is MORE. If the bottom row has extras, top is LESS. If everyone has a buddy, they are EQUAL.' Listen for children using the words spontaneously and tick the formative column.

steps.instruction: Whole-class debrief. Pull pairs back to the carpet with one of their cookie comparisons (their favourite — most surprising or trickiest). Each pair holds up their two plates and the room calls out 'MORE!', 'LESS!', or 'EQUAL!' before the pair confirms with the comparison strip. This rapid review locks in the three-word vocabulary as a class identity ('we are the people who use these three words').
steps.teacher_prompt: Say: 'Pair-A, hold up your plates. Class — eyes only, no counting out loud — is plate A more, less, or equal to plate B?' If the class is split, GREAT — line them up on the comparison strip together. The disagreement is the teaching moment.

differentiation.for_emerging: Emerging children stay with target numbers 3-5 at the compose station. Their cube count is reduced (5 cubes total) so the decomposition is fewer and clearer. At compare, they only use plates with 1-5 cookies each (which they can subitize from Lesson 4). They are assessed on building one decomposition correctly (not two) and on choosing the right comparison word for plates that differ by at least 2.
differentiation.for_extending: Extending children stretch to target numbers 8-10 (or 12, 15 if confident). At compose they look for ALL combinations for a target (e.g., 7 = 0+7, 1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1, 7+0 — the systematic ladder). At compare they use plates with quantities up to 20 and explain HOW MUCH MORE (not just 'more' but '6 more than 4 is 2 more, because 6 take away 4 is 2'). Some can predict before lining up: 'I think A has more because it has both rows of the ten-frame and B only has one row'.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Pre-teach the three comparison words with hand gestures: MORE (one hand high, one hand low), LESS (the reverse), EQUAL (two hands at the same height). Children echo the gesture every time the word is spoken. At compose, provide pre-snapped towers (e.g., a 5-tower, a 3-tower) so the child only has to choose which two go together to make the target, not build from scratch. At compare, allow drawing/pointing instead of saying the word. Pair with a strong-language partner who narrates aloud during the round.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: NO-PAPER, NO-PURCHASE PATH: skip the printed plates, paper cookies, comparison strip, and ten-frames. Use FINGERS for compose ('build 7' — child holds up 4 fingers on left + 3 on right, then 5+2, then 6+1; partner builds different splits). Use BODY LINE-UP for compare — children stand in TWO rows facing each other; pair off across rows; whoever has un-paired children at the end of the line is the MORE row, the one with no extras is LESS; if every child has a partner, the rows are EQUAL. Whole capstone runs on bodies and fingers — no purchased plates, no cookies, no ten-frames.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: FOUR signals because this lesson covers two expectations. (a) at compose, can the child build the target number with TWO different combinations on the first try? (b) at compose, do they use both colours strategically (red + yellow with a clear visual split), or do they grab any cubes? (c) at compare, do they line objects up on the comparison strip BEFORE picking a circle card, or do they pick a card visually without checking? (d) do they use the right word — MORE / LESS / EQUAL — in spontaneous talk with their partner, not just when prompted? Children who hit all four are securely composing AND comparing on A6.5 + A6.6.
formative_check.how_to_record: Per-child summative checklist with four columns: 'composes target two ways', 'uses two-colour split', 'lines up before comparing', 'uses correct comparison word'. Plus a portfolio sample: take a photo of each child's ten-frame at the moment they show two different decompositions. Plus a tally column for each comparison word the child used during the partner round (count how many times MORE, LESS, EQUAL came up).

consolidation.activity_name: Counting Crew Conversation — Same Number, Many Ways
discussion_prompts: Mae just asked us — when she has 4 cookies and Theo has 4 cookies, what word do we use? (Answer: equal.)
Theo wants to know — if you build 6 with three reds and three yellows, can your partner build 6 a different way? Show me with your fingers — how many ways could 6 be?

Buddy got two plates: one with 5 bones, one with 3. Which has more? How can you prove it WITHOUT counting one by one? (Look for: subitize each plate, then compare; or line them up and look for extras.)
When is it useful in real life to know if you have MORE or LESS? Think about lunch, recess, sharing. Tell your partner one example.
consolidation.exit_routine: Each child takes one number card 1-10 from the basket as they walk out and shows the teacher TWO ways to build that number with their fingers (e.g., for 5: shows 2+3, then 4+1). Teacher tallies on the 'Building Wall' chart who showed two ways instantly, who needed a prompt, and who could only show one way. The wall fills with names so the children see their progress as the unit closes.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Per-child summative checklist with the four indicators (composes target two ways, uses two-colour split, lines up before comparing, uses correct comparison word). Photo of each child's ten-frame showing two different decompositions of the same target. Tally of comparison-word usage during partner rounds. Exit-routine 'Building Wall' tally showing who can show two ways instantly. Each pair's final cookie comparison — photographed with the comparison strip — saved as portfolio evidence for A6.6.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 5 is the SUMMATIVE moment for the unit. A6.5 (compose/decompose to 10) and A6.6 (more/less/equal) are the most cognitively demanding expectations because they layer on top of A6.1-A6.4 — children need to identify numbers (A6.3), count forward and backward to verify (A6.2), subitize the smaller groups (A6.4), and understand quantity (A6.1) before they can compose or compare. The summative tier is appropriate because there are NO further unit lessons after this one — the assessment_suite stage will draw from this lesson's evidence. The four-column checklist plus photo portfolio gives a defensible report-card-level evidence base.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the Child Builds Two Compositions That Are Actually the Same — teaching the difference between 'flipped' and 'different' (Carpenter & Moser CGI, 1983; Resnick, 1983; Sarama & Clements, 2009; Mix, 2002)
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On A6.5 composing/decomposing to 10 and A6.6 comparing more/less/equal, the subtle K trap is the child who builds 7 as '4 red + 3 yellow' and then proudly shows their second composition as '3 red + 4 yellow' — same numbers, opposite colours.

Carpenter & Moser's (1983) CGI work classifies decompositions as instances of part-part-whole — the conceptual schema underlying both addition and subtraction. K children master decomposing IF they encounter the full decomposition lattice (0+7, 1+6, 2+5, 3+4 for 7), not just the colour-flipped pair. The 'Building Wall' debrief is engineered to make the lattice publicly visible.

Resnick (1983) names commutativity (3+4 = 4+3) as the conceptual move that lets K children understand 'colour flips are the same pair'. To an adult, 4+3 and 3+4 LOOK like two compositions; to the curriculum, they ARE two compositions (commutativity); but to a kindergartner, the question 'are these different ways to make 7?' is unsettled. The teacher's job is to AFFIRM both as legitimate (commutativity is real math) while ALSO pushing the child to find a TRULY different number pair so the decomposition lattice grows.

Sarama & Clements (2009) place comparing-by-matching (line up Plate A's cookies with Plate B's; whoever has extras is MORE) BEFORE comparing-by-counting in their trajectory. K children must master the matching strategy first — counting both plates and comparing the totals is a Grade-1 move. The comparison strip in Step 3 is a matching-strategy tool, not a counting tool, by design.

Mix (2002) showed that K children's success at cross-modal cardinality matching (matching a quantity in one modality — e.g., dot card — to a quantity in another — e.g., spoken number word) develops alongside subitizing AND counts as evidence of a unified cardinal concept. The exit_routine 'show TWO ways with fingers for a number card' tests this exact cross-modal match.

Why this matters: A6.5 and A6.6 are the most cognitively demanding K expectations because they layer on top of A6.1-A6.4. Children who finish K with only colour-flips don't have a decomposition lattice and arrive in Grade 1 still seeing addition as one-fact-at-a-time rather than a structured pattern. Step 2 (partner compose station) is where this trap shows up.

The script below covers exactly what to say and why colour-flipping counts but should not be the ONLY answer.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Compose station has a target number card 7 in front of the pair. The child has built two ten-frames: one shows 4 red + 3 yellow, the other shows 3 red + 4 yellow. The child is grinning, proud — they think they are done. Teacher walks up with the formative checklist clipboard.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script: Crouch beside the child. 'Wow, look at your two builds. Tell me about them.' Let them narrate. 'Four red and three yellow is seven. And three red and four yellow is seven.' Affirm GENEROUSLY first: 'YES — both are seven. The colour doesn't change the total. That is a real grown-up math idea — three plus four and four plus three are equal.' Pause. 'But I'm wondering — could you build seven WITHOUT using a 4 and a 3 at all? Could there be a way to make seven that has different NUMBERS of cubes, not just different colours?' Wait. The child will think. Sometimes they'll try 5+2 or 6+1; sometimes they'll need a hint. Hint: 'What if you only had ONE red cube? How many yellow would you need?' Wait. They count up: '6 yellow'. 'YES — 1 and 6 makes 7. That is a NEW way, with NEW numbers. Build it on a third ten-frame.' If you only have two ten-frames, sweep one of the colour-flipped builds away and rebuild as 1+6 in its place. 'Now you have three different ways: 4 and 3, 3 and 4, 1 and 6. The first two are colour-flips of each other — they're the SAME pair of numbers. The third is a DIFFERENT pair of numbers. Both kinds count as decomposing — but a really strong mathematician finds different number PAIRS, not just different colour orders.' Tick the 'composes target two ways' column. If the child gets to a different number pair on their own (e.g., 1+6 OR 5+2), tick TWO levels. If they only have colour flips, tick one level and note 'colour-flip only — re-prompt at decompose station next round'. By Lesson-5 standard, a child who can find at least one different number pair has mastered A6.5. A child who finds three different number pairs (e.g., 1+6, 2+5, 3+4) has surpassed it.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Builds 4+3 and 3+4 and stops. Treats colour-flip as the second way. Most common K starting point.
(Mid) After the prompt 'what if you only had 1 red?', builds 1+6 successfully but cannot find a third pair on their own without further prompts.
(Strong) Without prompting, finds 4+3, then 5+2, then 6+1, then 7+0. The decomposition lattice is forming.

(Stretched) Volunteers an EVEN-numbered observation: 'I bet 8 has different ones — 4 and 4 is the same colour split though, that's weird.' Generalises the lattice and notices the 'middle' decomposition. Flag as ready for Grade-1 stretch.
common_misconceptions: Colour flips are 'different ways'. (Most common at K. Pedagogically defensible — commutativity IS a valid second representation — but the child needs to also find pairs with different numbers, not just different colours.)

There's only one 'right' way to make 7. (Some children look for THE answer, like a sum problem. Affirm explicitly: there are EIGHT correct decompositions of 7 — 0+7 through 7+0 — and a kindergartner who finds even three is excellent.)

Bigger numbers have fewer decompositions. (Children sometimes think 9 is 'harder' so it must be more restrictive. The opposite is true — 9 has more decompositions than 5. The wall chart visually corrects this if you keep adding new decompositions to the 'Building Wall'.)
recovery_moves: Always affirm the colour-flip first. The child has done real math. THEN push for a different number pair so the decomposition lattice grows. Affirm-then-extend prevents the child from feeling 'wrong' for offering commutativity.
Use the '1-and-rest' prompt. 'What if you only had 1 red?' is a near-universal scaffolding move that gets children to a new decomposition without having to remember the full strategy.

Build the decomposition wall. As pairs find new decompositions, add them to the anchor chart. Children who have not yet found 5+2 will see another pair show 5+2 and copy it — peer learning is the fastest path through the decomposition lattice.

worksheet_brief.purpose: End-of-lesson summative consolidation. Children produce written evidence of composing a target number two ways AND of comparing two groups using MORE / LESS / EQUAL. This is the report-card-level worksheet — assessment_suite will draw from it. Goes home as both a take-home celebration AND a retained portfolio piece ('Show your family the THREE most important math words: more, less, equal').

parts_outline.task: Build the number 7 in TWO different ways using red and yellow cubes. Colour the squares to show what you built.
Look at Plate A and Plate B. Count the cookies on each. Circle MORE, LESS, or EQUAL to compare Plate A to Plate B.
Draw your own two plates of timbits. One plate has MORE than the other. Write how many are on each plate.
